talks.title: Why Security Awareness Training Fails, And What To Do Instead
talks.teaser: Demonstrates why Security Awareness Training Fails, And What To Do Instead and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: A WICCON presenter argues security awareness training fails to change behavior, using a purchased-but-unused barbell metaphor and offering three options including a psychology-based alternative.

Key Topics: The gap between awareness and behavior change; why annual training doesn't work; assume-breach as giving up on people; and psychology-informed alternatives to traditional awareness programs.

Technical Details: The speaker, a psychologist, demonstrates that knowing exercise is healthy and buying equipment doesn't produce behavior change—paralleling how security awareness doesn't prevent risky actions despite employee knowledge.

Takeaways: Security awareness training alone cannot change behavior. Organizations should adopt psychology-informed approaches or accept assume-breach rather than pretending training solves human risk.

talks.title: Azure DevOps Privilege Escalation: Pipeline Shenanigans
talks.teaser: Demonstrates azure DevOps Privilege Escalation: Pipeline Shenanigans and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Speaker and Scope

A security tester turned DevSecOps practitioner presents offensive Azure DevOps pipeline abuse. She contrasts a well-meaning project administrator with a compromised or malicious developer account.

Pipeline Building Blocks

Azure DevOps ties repositories to YAML-defined pipelines executed by agents. Agents often hold privileges developers lack, creating a first escalation path inside the project.

Service Connections as Secrets

Pipelines also use service connections storing credentials such as Azure service principals or third-party API keys. Those stored secrets form a second privilege-escalation avenue into cloud and tooling accounts.

Live Demo Setup

The demo project includes a pipeline with variable groups, hidden secrets referenced in build steps, and an Azure service connection for deployment. The speaker walks through where YAML, library variables, and service connections live before showing how a rogue developer might hijack them.

talks.title: Breaking In: A Journey Through The Cybersecurity Hiring Maze
talks.teaser: Explores breaking In: A Journey Through The Cybersecurity Hiring Maze and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The hiring paradox

A newcomer to cyber security describes leaving repetitive IT QA work for the field amid loud skills-gap messaging—thousands of Dutch vacancies—yet experiencing repeated rejection when applying as a career changer.

Personal path

Background spans healthcare account management, software quality assurance, party events, CEH training, and a short pentest internship that proved too screen-heavy. Five months at 32 hours per week of searching finally yielded a SOC consultant role.

Community help vs barriers

The security community offered generous informational conversations even when not hiring. Major blockers included job posts listing many expensive certifications (CISSP, CISM, OSEP) far above entry level, and junior titles requiring prior experience. She advises talk-first-certify-later and clearer preferred-certificate labeling.

talks.title: Embedded AI: Evolving Attack Surface And Ways To Defend Them
talks.teaser: Presents embedded AI: Evolving Attack Surface And Ways To Defend Them and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Beyond the AI Buzzword

This WICCON talk distinguishes traditional AI, generative AI, and embedded AI—models that run at the edge without sending data to remote servers. That local processing embeds intelligence directly into workflows, often with little human validation of outputs.

## Growing Attack Surface

The speaker reviews market growth drivers and emerging risks: large interconnected datasets tied to sensitive information, reduced human oversight, and new integration points attackers can abuse. Edge AI expands the blast radius when models or their pipelines are compromised.

## Real-World Example: MCP

A highlighted case is the Model Context Protocol (MCP), rapidly adopted to connect AI systems to internal data. An RCE flaw (since patched) allowed arbitrary command execution when developers visited malicious sites, stemming from weak input validation and missing authorization checks—a pattern seen across many AI deployments.

## Defensive Guidance

Organizations should treat AI components like any other critical software: enforce access controls, validate inputs, monitor model behavior, and assess embedded deployments separately from cloud LLM use cases. Security must keep pace with how fast AI is being wired into production systems.

talks.title: Inside The CRA Standardisation Trenches: Our Struggle To Harmonise
talks.teaser: Examines inside The CRA Standardisation Trenches: enterprise Struggle To Harmonise and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security consultant Raoka Vizu (Bureau of Cyber Security) and industrial automation specialist Wendy Togs (Omron) share an inside look at drafting the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) standards. Both speakers are active members of CEN-CENELEC Working Group 9, the group responsible for developing horizontal harmonized standards that apply across all products with digital elements. The presentation addresses what the CRA requires, the implications for manufacturers and software developers, and the significant hurdles faced when drafting horizontal standards under aggressive timelines.

### Key Topics
- **Scope and Nature of the CRA**: The CRA targets nearly all products with digital elements, encompassing both hardware and software (including supporting tools and commercial software connecting to operating systems), requiring secure-by-design principles throughout product lifecycles.
- **Product Classification & Conformity**: Products are divided into default/standard products (roughly 90% of the market) and special categories outlined in Annex 3 (important products, classes 1 and 2) and Annex 4 (critical products). Special classes dictate conformity assessment methods, ranging from self-assessment using harmonized standards to mandatory third-party assessments or European cybersecurity certification (such as Common Criteria).
- **Regulatory Interplay**: Sectors with specific existing cyber requirements (automotive, medical, aviation, maritime) have exclusions, but products falling outside those specific boundaries (e.g., standard firewalls in hospitals) still fall into the CRA. The CRA also aligns with NIS 2 requirements for critical infrastructure suppliers and complements frameworks like the AI Act under the New Legislative Framework.
- **Harmonized Standards Mandate**: Standards developed by CEN-CENELEC and ETSI under European Commission standardization requests provide a presumption of conformity required for the CE mark.

### Technical Details & Implementation Challenges
- **Strict Timelines**: The CRA entered into force in December 2024. Reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe cybersecurity incidents become mandatory on September 11, 2026 (requiring notification to national CSIRTs and ENISA's single reporting platform). The entire regulation and its technical requirements become mandatory on December 11, 2027.
- **Process vs. Product Conformity**: Harmonized standards face structural contradictions. For example, essential requirements mandate secure development processes, yet CE marks apply strictly to the end product. Other legal demands, such as providing product security updates free of charge, cannot be written directly into a technical standard, complicating presumption of conformity.
- **Reaching Consensus Under Time Pressure**: While mature standards typically take roughly five years to reach consensus, Working Group 9 delivered a first draft in May after a December standardization request and reached the inquiry stage within months. Reconciling varied stakeholder needs—from multinational corporations with established frameworks like IEC 62443 to small-and-medium enterprises (SMEs) and open-source contributors—proves exceptionally difficult.

### Takeaways
Manufacturers cannot delay preparation while waiting for finalized harmonized standards. By December 11, 2027, products lacking a CE mark cannot be placed on the EU market. Although the CRA does not directly regulate non-commercial open-source projects, manufacturers integrating open-source or third-party components remain liable for ensuring long-term compliance. The speakers urge industry practitioners, software developers, and SMEs to participate directly in their national standardization bodies and comment during the standard's inquiry phase.
